verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION MEMO — C-01
Subject: Citation of NBS/NIST Technical Note 904 ('Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response') as the source of a design basic wind speed; and the content of the 25 Hz passage.

=====================================================================
0. CONSTRAINT HONORED (ASK 1)
=====================================================================
Evidence base for this determination is restricted to the supplied page passages. What was actually supplied and used:

From NBS TN 904 (Shaver, 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response', NBS TN 904, published 1976, doi 10.6028/NBS.TN.904):
 (a) Title page / abstract / keywords;
 (b) Table of contents;
 (c) Section 1, Introduction;
 (d) Section 2, Background;
 (e) Section 4, Data Reduction and Analysis (the passage containing '25 Hz').

From other, distinct documents in the same corpus (used only to show what a legitimate wind-speed source looks like, NOT as evidence about TN 904):
 (f) NBS Building Science Series 100-2 — passages defining 'basic design wind speed' by CDF / mean recurrence interval and citing ANSI A58.1;
 (g) NBS TN 900 — a separate floor-vibration note that cites TN 904.

Limitation stated up front: the TN 904 evidence is a page excerpt set, not the whole note. The scope conclusion below therefore rests on the note's own abstract, keywords and table of contents (which define the note's subject) plus the absence of any wind content in every supplied page — not on a page-by-page exhaustion of a document I was not given in full. That is sufficient for the verdict, and the residual is called out in §5.

=====================================================================
1. VERDICT (ASK 2): NO — TN 904 CANNOT BE USED AS THE SOURCE FOR A DESIGN BASIC WIND SPEED
=====================================================================
Determination: NOT USABLE. The citation in the compliance file is defective and must be struck and replaced (see §4).

Grounds, each traceable to a supplied passage:

R1 — Stated scope excludes wind. The abstract describes the work as 'A new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations ... based on the assumption that human activity, which produces the vibration, and human response to vibration are random variables.' The subject is floor vibration serviceability. Wind is never named as a subject of the note.

R2 — The note's own index of subjects excludes wind. The keyword list is: 'Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response; random process; spectral analysis; vibration.' No wind, no wind load, no wind speed, no meteorology, no return period.

R3 — The table of contents excludes wind. Sections are: 1 Introduction; 2 Background; 3 Approach to Problem; 4 Data Reduction and Analysis; 5 Damping; 6 Human Response to Vibration; 7 Summary; 8 References; 9 Appendix A: Field Test; 10 Appendix B: Computer Program. There is no wind section, no climatic section, no load section.

R4 — The introduction frames the problem as deflection-based serviceability design of floors under 'a given design load', with human activity as the dynamic source: 'Historically, the design of floor systems for serviceability has been based on limiting the deflection that can occur for a given design load ... It was believed by most engineers that this design procedure indirectly accounted for the effect of human activity on floor systems which could produce quite perceptible and annoying vibrations for other human occupants.' The forcing function under study is human footfall/activity, not wind.

R5 — No numeric wind speed appears anywhere in the supplied pages. Not one value in m/s, km/h or mph, and no definition of a basic design wind speed, in any supplied TN 904 passage. A source that contains no such value cannot be the source of a value.

R6 — The definition the compliance file needs belongs to a code, not to this note. In the supplied corpus the term is defined in a different document (NBS BSS 100-2): '... be estimated to characterize the probabilistic behavior of the largest yearly wind speeds. The basic design wind speed is then defined as the speed corresponding to a specified value F0 of the CDF or, equivalently (in view of the relation N = 1/(1-F0) in which N = mean recurrence interval), as the speed corresponding to a specified mean recurrence interval. For example, the American National Standard A58.1 [1] specifies that a basic design wind speed corresponding to a 50-year mean recurrence interval (i.e., to a value F0 of the CDF equal to 0.98, or to a probability of exceedance of the basic wind speed in any one year equal to 0.02) be used in designing all permanent structures, except those structures with an unusually high degree of hazard to life and property in case of failure, for which a 100-year mean recurrence interval (F0 = 0.99) must be used, and structures having no human occupants or where there is negligible risk to human life, for which a 25-year mean recurrence (F0 = 0.96) may be used.' Design basic wind speed is thus a code-defined, risk-category-dependent, return-period statistic. TN 904 is a research note on human perception of floor vibration; it has no standing to supply it, and supplies no number for it.

R7 — Even the note that cites TN 904 does not cite it for wind. NBS TN 900, in the supplied passage, cites 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response [21]' as a study of the random forcing function and human response in floor vibration. That is corroboration of TN 904's actual subject and of the correct use of the citation.

=====================================================================
2. CONTENT OF THE 25 Hz PASSAGE (ASK 3)
=====================================================================
Answer: 25 Hz. The passage is a signal-conditioning statement about the measurement chain, not a wind speed, not a design criterion, and not a human-perception frequency limit.

Verbatim (supplied rendering, TN 904 p. 7/8):
  'signal conditioning equipment all input above 2 5 Hz has been removed thus accounting for the low energy content above this value.
   The acceleration record was sampled every 160 ms which is equivalent, because of a difference in record and playback speed of the analog data tape, to a 10 ms sampling rate in real time. At the 10 ms real time sampling rate, 1191 samples were taken thus producing a natural frequency spacing of 0.084 Hz in the Fourier transform. The modulus of the spectral decomposition has been plotted at every 0.5 Hz.
   An examination of Figure 3 indicates that significant amounts of energy occurs in the range of 15-25 Hz with a pronounced peak at 18 Hz which is the fundamental frequency for the floor tested. The existence of energy in this range indicates that a vibrating floor system is capable of inducing a human response to vibration at frequencies other than the lowest natural frequency of the system. Thus, test procedures which determine the vibration level only at the fundamental frequency for the floor system may exclude significant energy levels at other frequencies.'

Note on transcription: one supplied rendering OCRs the figure as '2 5 Hz'; a second supplied rendering of the same page reads '25 Hz'. The correct reading is 25 Hz.

Plain-language reading, element by element:
- 'all input above 25 Hz has been removed' = a 25 Hz low-pass filter (anti-alias / noise-band limit) was applied in signal conditioning to the acceleration record. Content above 25 Hz was discarded.
- Rationale given in the text itself: 'accounting for the low energy content above this value' — i.e., little useful signal was expected above 25 Hz, so it was filtered out rather than analyzed.
- Acquisition parameters: analog tape replay at 160 ms per sample, equivalent to 10 ms per sample in real time after tape-speed correction; 1191 samples; Fourier frequency spacing 0.084 Hz; spectral modulus plotted every 0.5 Hz.
- Physical finding: significant energy in the 15-25 Hz band, with a pronounced peak at 18 Hz = the fundamental frequency of the floor tested.
- Engineering point being made: a floor can excite human response at frequencies other than its lowest natural frequency, so test procedures that measure only at the fundamental may miss significant energy at other frequencies.

What the passage is NOT (each a rejection of a plausible misreading):
- It is NOT a wind speed. '25 Hz' is a frequency, not a velocity; the units are incompatible and no wind quantity appears on the page.
- It is NOT a design basic wind speed, nor any input to one.
- It is NOT a 25-year mean recurrence interval. The 25-year MRI (F0 = 0.96) is a wind-statistics quantity from the *other* document (BSS 100-2, quoting ANSI A58.1) and has nothing to do with this page. See §3.
- It is NOT a code-mandated human-perception threshold or a pass/fail acceptance limit for floor vibration. It is a description of the analyzer's filter setting and the resulting spectrum; the note's own position is that the acceptance link is missing ('The missing link at this time is a means of transforming the energy ...').

=====================================================================
3. LIKELY ROOT CAUSE OF THE CITATION ERROR (HYPOTHESIS — TO BE CONFIRMED, NOT RELIED ON)
=====================================================================
The only '25' in the supplied wind material is the 25-year mean recurrence interval applicable to 'structures having no human occupants or where there is negligible risk to human life' (F0 = 0.96). The only '25' in the supplied TN 904 material is the 25 Hz filter cutoff on a page that also discusses human response. A citation that pairs a wind quantity with a human-response document is consistent with these two being conflated. Treat this as a lead to check against the compliance file's actual citation text; do not record it as a finding.

=====================================================================
4. REQUIRED CORRECTIVE ACTIONS ON THE COMPLIANCE FILE
=====================================================================
C1. Strike the NBS TN 904 citation from the design-basic-wind-speed entry. Mark it 'superseded — incorrect source' rather than deleting silently, so the review trail is preserved.
C2. Re-source the value from the governing code/standard adopted by the jurisdiction (the ANSI A58.1 lineage, i.e. the ASCE 7 edition invoked by the applicable building code), citing edition, figure/table or map, and the risk category / mean recurrence interval used. Confirm the edition and MRI against the adopted code — do not carry the 50/100/25-year values in §1 R6 forward as current; they are quoted from a 1970s NBS document and modern editions differ by risk category.
C3. If a non-code technical reference is retained for any purpose, retain TN 904 only for what it actually supports: floor-vibration serviceability and human response — and cite it there, alongside TN 900 where that note is used.
C4. Add a check to the citation QA: every wind-speed citation must resolve to a document whose scope includes wind loading and must carry an MRI/risk-category statement. TN 904 fails both tests.
C5. If any '25' remains in the wind entry, verify in writing that it denotes a 25-year mean recurrence interval and not a 25 Hz frequency.

=====================================================================
5. RESIDUAL / LIMITATIONS
=====================================================================
- The TN 904 evidence is a page excerpt set. The verdict does not depend on the missing pages: the abstract, keyword list and table of contents define the note's subject, and no supplied page carries wind content. If a reviewer requires page-by-page exhaustion, obtain the full note (NBS TN 904, 1976, 20-odd pages, doi 10.6028/NBS.TN.904) and confirm; the verdict is not expected to change.
- The compliance file's actual citation text and the specific wind speed value it attributes to the note were not supplied and are not restated here. C1-C5 are written to be executable once that text is in hand.
- The governing code edition and jurisdiction were not supplied; C2 is therefore framed as a procedure rather than a fixed citation.

verdict.summary:
CITATION FINDING — NBS/NIST Technical Note 904 (Shaver, 1976), 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response', cited in a compliance file as the source for a design basic wind speed.

1. VERDICT (ask 2): NO. NBS TN 904 cannot be used as the source for a design basic wind speed. The supplied passages establish that the note's subject is the serviceability of floor systems under human activity: 'A new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations is presented based on the assumption that human activity, which produces the vibration, and human response to vibration are random variables. Techniques for data reduction are discussed and a detailed description of one approach is given along with the associated computer programs. Data from floor vibrations is compared with current criteria for human response.' Its listed key words are 'Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response; random process; spectral analysis; vibration.' Its contents are Introduction, Background, Approach to Problem, Data Reduction and Analysis, Damping, Human Response to Vibration, Summary, References, Appendix A (Field Test), and Appendix B (Computer Program). None of the supplied passages contains any wind speed value, any wind loading provision, any averaging interval for a wind speed (e.g., a 3-second gust), any mph or m/s figure, or any definition of the term 'design basic wind speed'. Consequently there is no content in the supplied passages from which a design basic wind speed could be derived, quoted, or attributed to TN 904.

2. WHAT THE 25 Hz PASSAGE ACTUALLY SAYS (ask 3): In the data-reduction and analysis section, discussing Figure 3 of the field test, the note states that the spectral 'decomposition has been plotted at every 0.5 Hz', and then: 'An examination of Figure 3 indicates that significant amounts of energy occurs in the range of 15-25 Hz with a pronounced peak at 18 Hz which is the fundamental frequency for the floor tested. The existence of energy in this range indicates that a vibrating floor system is capable of inducing a human response to vibration at frequencies other than the lowest natural frequency of the system. Thus, test procedures which determine the vibration level only at the fundamental frequency for the floor system may exclude significant energy levels at other frequencies.' The passage then notes that a means of converting those energy levels to rms acceleration at the same frequency was still missing, and that rms acceleration for the record is associated with the lowest natural frequency for comparison with human response criteria (done in section 6).

Interpretation for the compliance file: the '25 Hz' figure is the UPPER BOUND OF A VIBRATION-FREQUENCY RANGE (15–25 Hz) in the power/spectral decomposition of floor acceleration response, with the notable peak at 18 Hz identified as the tested floor's fundamental frequency. The unit is hertz (cycles per second of structural vibration). It is not a speed, not wind-related, not a gust figure, and carries no velocity unit. If the compliance file treats '25' as a wind speed magnitude (e.g., 25 mph) or as anything other than a vibration frequency, that is a misreading of the source.

3. DOCUMENTATION OF THE DISCREPANCY (for the compliance record): The citation of TN 904 for a design basic wind speed is erroneous on its face. Design basic wind speed is a defined wind-climate parameter of wind-loading standards and building codes (the supplied SP 457-1 wind passage, for instance, is explicitly framed around 'the ANSI A58.1 Standard' assumption on extreme wind speeds and is a different document — not TN 904). Correct procedure: (a) strike TN 904 as the authority for any design basic wind speed; (b) replace it with the governing wind-loading standard or building code edition actually adopted for the project (the citation must identify the standard, edition, the wind speed's averaging interval and unit, the risk category / mean recurrence interval, and the applicable exposure and location), which the supplied passages do not supply and which therefore must come from the compliance file's own governing code, not from TN 904; (c) verify whether '25' was transcribed from the 15–25 Hz vibration range and, if so, remove it from any wind-speed field; (d) re-verify every other figure in the file that shares the same TN 904 citation line, since the same transcription error may have propagated. No numeric design basic wind speed is stated anywhere in the supplied passages, and none is asserted here; any value appearing in the compliance file attributed to TN 904 is unsupported by the cited source.

verdict.summary:
STRUCTURAL ENGINEERING REVIEW MEMORANDUM
Subject: Adequacy of NBS/NIST Technical Note 904 ('Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response') as the cited source for a design basic wind speed in the compliance file
Review basis: the supplied page passages only (Ask 1 constraint)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DEFINITION OF THE QUANTITY BEING SUBSTANTIATED
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
The compliance file must substantiate a DESIGN BASIC WIND SPEED. From the supplied code passages, that term has a single, code-specific meaning and nothing else:

  'Basic Wind Speed (V): The area Basic wind speed obtained from Figures 26.5-1A through 26.5-1D, mi/h (m/s); the basic wind speed corresponds to a 3-second gust at 33 feet (10 meters) above the ground in Exposure Category C.' (FEMA design guide quoting ASCE 7-22)

  'The basic wind speed, V, in mph, for the determination of the wind loads shall be determined by Figures 1609.3(1) through 1609.3(4).' ... 'Values are 3-second gust wind speeds in miles per hour (m/s) at 33 feet (10 m) above ground for Exposure Category C.' ... 'Location-specific basic wind speeds shall be determined using the ASCE Wind Design Geodatabase.' (TWIA Building Code 2024 Sec. 1609.3 and Fig. 1609.3(1) notes)

So the required deliverable from any cited source is one of: a mapped/contoured basic wind speed, a site-specific value from the ASCE Wind Design Geodatabase (asce7hazardtool.online) or approved equivalent, or a defensible derivation of the same. Any source offered must supply that, at the adopted code edition.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. ASK 1 - THE EVIDENTIARY UNIVERSE (constraint)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
The supplied passages are registered below. Every conclusion in this memo is drawn from these and only these.

P1  nist.gov publication record for 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response' - author James R. Shaver, published January 1, 1976, report number NBS TN 904, DOI 10.6028/NBS.TN.904. Bibliographic only.
P2  nvlpubs TN 904 PDF - front matter, abstract, table of contents, Section 1 Introduction.
    Abstract: 'A new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations is presented based on the assumption that human activity, which produces the vibration, and human response to vibration are random variables. Techniques for data reduction are discussed ... Data from floor vibrations is compared with current criteria for human response.'
    Key words: 'Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response; random process; spectral analysis; vibration.'
P3  nvlpubs TN 904 PDF - Introduction/Body: perceptible floor vibration, forcing function for human activity, deterministic vs. random variables.
P4  nvlpubs TN 904 PDF - Section 7 Summary: spectral analysis chosen over time history; 'A computationally efficient procedure for obtaining the Fourier spectrum is given along with the associated computer software'; human reaction to externally applied vertical transient vibration compared with 'a proposed standard for vibration and shock limits for occupants of buildings'.
P5  govinfo.gov content-details page for the same report - series NBSIR, publication number 75-951, issued 1975, Commerce Department.
P6  govinfo.gov PDF of the report - abstract, TOC, Introduction, and Summary (duplicate text of P2-P4 with different pagination).
P7  up.codes - Texas Windstorm Insurance Association Building Code 2024, Sec. 1609.3 Basic Wind Speed, Figs 1609.3(1)-(4), Sec. 1609.3.1 Wind Speed Conversion.
P8  fema.gov - Design Guide for New Tornado Load Requirements in ASCE 7-22: definitions of Basic Wind Speed (V), ASCE 7 Hazard Tool, performance-based procedures.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. ASK 2 - VERDICT: CAN TN 904 BE USED AS THE SOURCE FOR A DESIGN BASIC WIND SPEED?
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
VERDICT: NO.

Grounds, each independently sufficient and each read directly from the supplied passages:

(a) Subject matter is wrong. The note is, in its own words, about 'perceptible floor vibrations' and 'human response to vibration' (P2, P3), with the stated purpose of treating human activity and human response as random variables and applying spectral analysis to floor vibration records (P4). No supplied passage addresses wind, wind loading, wind climate, terrain exposure, gust durations, or return periods as they relate to wind.

(b) No wind speed value, map, or derivation appears anywhere in the note's supplied content. The note's quantitative content in the supplied pages is methodological: data reduction, Fourier spectrum computation, damping, human response criteria (P2, P4). A source that contains no wind speed cannot be the source for a wind speed.

(c) The document is not a loading standard and predates the quantity's modern definition. P1 and P5 date it to 1975-1976 (NBSIR 75-951 / NBS TN 904). The basic wind speed the compliance file needs is defined by ASCE 7 Figs 26.5-1A-D / IBC-TWIA Figs 1609.3(1)-(4) as a 3-second gust at 33 ft (10 m) in Exposure Category C, with location-specific values from the ASCE Wind Design Geodatabase (P7, P8). TN 904 neither is nor incorporates that definition.

(d) The note's own framing points the other way. Its summary compares floor-vibration data against 'a proposed standard for vibration and shock limits for occupants of buildings' (P4) - a serviceability/human-comfort criterion. Wind-speed mapping is a load-hazard input, not a comfort criterion.

CHARACTER OF THE ERROR: This is a WRONG-DOCUMENT citation, not a page-scope technicality. It is not cured by citing additional pages of TN 904, because no page of a floor-vibration/human-response note supplies a code-mapped basic wind speed. The verdict would change only on production of a supplied passage from TN 904 that states a wind speed value or a wind-speed map/derivation - and no such passage was supplied.

CORRECTIVE ACTION: Strike TN 904 as the wind-speed source. Cite instead the basic wind speed figure or geodatabase output of the adopted code edition - e.g. ASCE 7-22 Figs 26.5-1A through 26.5-1D, or IBC/TWIA 2024 Figs 1609.3(1) through 1609.3(4) matched to the structure's Risk Category, with the site-specific value taken from the ASCE 7 Hazard Tool (asce7hazardtool.online) or approved equivalent. If the file also cites TN 904 for floor-vibration serviceability, that use is proper and should be retained, but it must be presented as a vibration criterion and must not be labeled or relied upon as a wind-speed source.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. ASK 3 - WHAT DOES THE 25 Hz PASSAGE ACTUALLY SAY?
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
STATUS: CANNOT BE ANSWERED FROM THE SUPPLIED PASSAGES.

Findings of the text search of P1-P8: the strings '25', 'Hz', 'hertz', and 'cycles per second' do not occur in any supplied passage. There is therefore no 25 Hz passage in the record supplied to me, and I will not reconstruct, paraphrase, or 'quote from memory' a passage that is not in evidence. Doing so would inject an unverifiable quotation into a compliance file - the precise defect this review is meant to catch.

What the supplied passages DO establish about the note's frequency content, stated at the level of generality the passages actually support:
  - 'Spectral analysis is chosen over time, history, as the method for analyzing floor vibration data.' (P4)
  - 'A computationally efficient procedure for obtaining the Fourier spectrum is given along with the associated computer software.' (P4)
  - The note treats damping (TOC, P2/P6) and 'human reaction to externally applied vertical transient vibration' (P4).
  - The results are compared with 'a proposed standard for vibration and shock limits for occupants of buildings' (P4).
No frequency limit, cutoff, or threshold value is quantified in any supplied passage.

TO CLOSE ASK 3, the reviewer must supply the page image or verbatim text of the passage containing '25 Hz'. On receipt, handle it as follows:
  1. Quote it verbatim, with page number, and identify which section it sits in (Introduction / Data Reduction and Analysis / Damping / Human Response to Vibration / Summary).
  2. State its context explicitly - whether 25 Hz is (i) an upper frequency bound of a spectral analysis or sampling/anti-alias limit, (ii) a frequency above which human response to vibration is not evaluated, (iii) a floor system's natural frequency, or (iv) something else.
  3. Note the consequence for the compliance file: whichever of (i)-(iv) it is, it is a VIBRATION-SERVICEABILITY parameter. It has no path to a design basic wind speed. Its presence in the note therefore cannot rescue the citation in Ask 2; at most it shows the filer read a frequency figure out of a vibration criterion and misapplied it.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. LIMITS OF THIS REVIEW
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
This review is confined to the supplied passages, as instructed. I did not search the note's full text, and the filer may be relying on a page not supplied. That limitation does not affect the Ask 2 verdict: even a complete reading of a 1976 floor-vibration/human-response note cannot yield the code-defined basic wind speed, because the note does not contain wind hazard data and is not a loading standard. The limitation does affect Ask 3, which is why it is recorded as blocked rather than answered.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. DISPOSITION SUMMARY
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ask 1 (constraint): satisfied - all findings traced to passages P1-P8 above.
Ask 2 (verdict): NO - TN 904 cannot serve as the source for a design basic wind speed. Wrong-document citation. Replace with the adopted code's basic wind speed figure or ASCE 7 Hazard Tool output.
Ask 3 (value): BLOCKED - no 25 Hz passage exists in the supplied record; verbatim text required before any statement can be made.
